one_sentence_story: In 2006, Stanislas Dehaene, Jean-Pierre Changeux, and Lionel Naccache formulated the Global Neuronal Workspace model — proving unconscious sensory signals stay trapped in local early cortex (<200 ms), whereas conscious awareness erupts around ~270–300 ms via a sudden all-or-none 'Global Ignition' across long-range prefrontal-parietal tracts that broadcasts one thought to memory, language, and planning at once.
so_what_for_you: Respect the biological physics of your **Global Workspace**: while dozens of sensory routines run unconsciously in parallel, your **conscious 300-ms broadcast stage holds only ONE rich thought at a time** — guard single-task quiet blocks whenever real insight matters.

jargon_map.plain: long-range reciprocal network of prefrontal and parietal cortical neurons whose white-matter axons broadcast one selected representation to the entire brain
jargon_map.analogy: putting one local microphone up to the stadium loudspeaker so every section hears it at once

jargon_map.plain: Dehaene's 3-way map: too weak to ever broadcast (Subliminal), strong enough yet missed while the stage is busy (Preconscious), vs globally broadcast (Conscious)
jargon_map.analogy: a whisper outside the door, a caller on hold while you're on another line, and the speaker live on stage

jargon_map.plain: sudden nonlinear step-up ~270–300 ms after stimulus onset where activity leaps from local visual areas into sustained frontoparietal sharing
jargon_map.analogy: crossing the tipping point where a local hum locks an entire bridge into unified resonance

jargon_map.plain: pre-registered open test pitting Dehaene's frontoparietal GNW against Tononi's posterior IIT across fMRI, MEG, and intracranial recordings
jargon_map.analogy: two rival architects co-designing one stress test to see which beam bends
